newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian markets keep eyes peeled for U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Asian markets keep eyes peeled for U.S. data.

text.p: Stock market activity in Asia was expected to be cautious despite the end of a four-session losing streak on Wall Street on Friday, with a slew of economic data due from the United States in the week ahead.

The U.S. Employment Cost Index, the National Association of Purchasing Managers' index and the October jobs report, October consumer confidence and third quarter preliminary gross domestic product figures are due in the week, among others.

Sentiment in Japan was expected to remain weak on political uncertainty, with potential coalition partners seeking a high price from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto as he struggled to secure a majority in the hung parliament.
In Hong Kong further consolidation was seen after the Hang Seng's recent dizzying rise, but brokers were not worried that the Dow's weakness would shake confidence in the longer-term outlook.
TOKYO - Any possible rebound in the week ahead after a five-day losing streak could be limited by feeble market sentiment, brokers said.

"Technical alarms are beginning to clang, signalling that the index is being oversold, so further falls should be limited," Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities. "But the investor mood is so chilly, gains may be hard to accumulate."

Most market sources said the Nikkei 225 was likely to be locked in a 20,500 to 21,500 range, with the benchmark toeing the downside. On Friday the Nikkei shed 263.52 points or 1.25 percent to 20,739.97, making for a weekly loss of more than 870 points or four percent.
HONG KONG - Hong Kong stocks appear set for a much-needed pullback, with further consolidation of as much as 200 points in the index a positive development, brokers said.

"The Hong Kong market climbed to record highs in a short time and is quite overbought. It is also more volatile at this level and prone to profit-taking," said Percy Au-Young, director of research at DBS Securities Hong Kong Ltd.

The Hang Seng Index closed down 85.19 points at 12,388.38 on Friday. Over the four-day week, the index eased at total of 121.64 points or 1.00 percent. Turnover remained robust with daily turnover averaging HK$6.84 billion.
BANGKOK - The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index is expected to fall on continued concerns by investors over possible cashflow problems by property firms and their inability to settle debts.

"Talk in the market about the cashflow problems are expected to continue to affect market sentiment in the week ahead. The decline on Wall Street this week also affected the market here," said Thanadech Mahapokai of Book Club Finance.
The SET index closed at 938.30 points on Friday, compared to 948.09 last Friday.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are expected to seek direction from first-half results of major companies due in the week ahead after a volatile week of trade, dealers said.
An easier credit policy for the first half of 1996/97 announced on October 19 by the central bank buoyed prices with the index jumping over 6.7 percent in two straight sessions.
Profit-taking at higher levels wiped out market gains, as the Bombay share index ended 120.45 points, or 3.8 percent, higher at 3,250.66 in the week to Friday.
COLOMBO - Sri Lanka stocks, which eased on profit-taking, are expected to mark time in a direction-less market, brokers said.
"The index will stay about five to 10 points above or below 600 until there is some clear direction," said Prasanna Chandrasekera of brokerage John Keells.
Traders expect the budget on November 6 to provide the direction the market is waiting for.
The all share closed at 600.05 points on Friday, 7.99 points lower than the previous week.
DHAKA - Dhaka stocks rallied in all but one session in the past week after investors shrugged off confusion about a restriction on price movement.

"The market stabilised in the week. But I am not sure about the week ahead after news that the Securities and Exchange Commission plans to set up a central depository system. There is a huge kerb market out there," said one broker.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange benchmark index gained 92.64 points to close at 2,193.80 in the week ending on Thursday. Friday is the Moslem weekend.
JAKARTA - Share prices are likely to move in a narrow range as many brokers opt for short-term trades in anticipation of next month's initial public offering by Bank Negara Indonesia, brokers said.
"Overall trade will be relatively slow with activity focused on speculative buying of some secondaries," said an analyst with a local brokerage.

A foreign broker said possible small foreign buying of heavyweight Astra International could give a positive tone to broader market sentiment. "After its excellent nine-month results there is still room for the price to rise," he added.
On Friday, Jakarta's composite index closed at 571.34 points, against last week's close of 570.20 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - Analysts expect the Malaysian bourse to start weaker but later pick up steam in the week ahead.
"We anticipate something of a disappointment when trading starts on Monday," said John Engle, managing director of HG Asia in Kuala Lumpur. Malaysia unveiled its 1997 budget on Friday.
"Property stocks should feel the impact of the 100,000 ringgit levy on foreigners buying residential properties not being lifted.
"Also, credit card issuers, specifically MBf, could also be hit by the imposition of the 50 ringgit annual tax on all types of credit cards," he added.
Week-on-week, the composite index was down 2.65 points at 1172.95, while the second board climbed 6.71 points to 631.36.
MANILA - Philippine stocks are expected to suffer declines on follow-through selling after the sharp fall of Philippine National Bank (PNB) on Friday, analysts said.

"PNB was a shocker and next week we will still see its negative aftershocks," said Joey Salceda, president of SBC Warburg. On Friday, PNB plummetted 87.50 pesos, or 21.34 percent, to 322.50 after posting disappointing nine-month results.
According to Noel Reyes, research head at Anscor Hagedorn Securities, immediate support is seen at 2,950 points.
The main index slid 137.13 points, or 4.62 percent, to 2,962.60 points on Friday versus 3,099.73 a week ago.
SEOUL - South Korean shares are expected to be mixed as bargain hunters struggle with uncertain sentiment, brokers said.
"It will be very difficult to predict what will happen on Monday because trading has been so directionless," said Ha Yong-hyun, a Hyundai Securities broker.
Brokers said investors feared that an anticipated interest rate cut would be delayed due to a huge amount of bond issues expected next month.
On Friday, the composite index closed at 793.78, down 36.47 points, or 4.4 percent, from last Friday's closing of 830.25. It eased a further 1,97 points in Saturday's half-day trade.
SINGAPORE - The market could rise further in the week ahead as investors have factored in the slowdown in the country's economic growth, dealers said.
However, they cautioned that the upside was likely to be capped at 2,150 as fundamentals had not changed and the recent recovery in the straits times industrials index was largely technical.
"We did see some institutions nibbling blue chips and diversified counters but there was no feeding frenzy," one dealer said.
The index ended up 17.59 points at 2,077.20 on Friday against 2,182.31 a week ago.

SYDNEY - Dealers said the Australian share market looked shaky in the near term as nervous investors, wary of Wall Street weakness and disappointed by the non-arrival of an interest rate cut on Friday, looked set to sell further.

Key inflation and wages data during the week failed to provoke the Reserve Bank of Australia into a rate cut and this accelerated Friday's losses, despite the benchmark all ordinaries index closing at a record level on Thursday.
"The market is very apprehensive. It has certainly got a case of the hippie-hippie shakes," said dealer Paul Ford of Shaw Stockbroking.
On Friday the index slumped 42.4 points to 2,335.2, erasing all of Thursday's record-breaking gains.
TAIPEI - Taiwan shares are expected to continue to consolidate in a narrow range in cautious trade, brokers said.
"Cheaper issues and blue chips may rise in turn to support the market but major movements are unlikely," said Albert Lin of Golden Securities.

The stock market was closed on Friday and Saturday for national holidays. On Thursday, the index ended at 6,458.91, compared with 6,494.34 last Thursday and 6,431.95 on Saturday. It is expected to move between 6,400 and 6,500 points in the week ahead.
WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares are expected to hold steady after ending the week with an inevitable shakeout of the previous week's 111-point rally, brokers said.
But they said the main caveat was what might happen in the United States.

Don Turkington at Cavill White Securities said he expected the market to maintain a reasonable tone next week after a period of consolidation. "The Dow seems to be going through a reasonably sizeable correction at the moment, so that could take some of the drive out of this market," he said.
The benchmark NZSE-40 capital index ended at 2,327.20, down 33.88 points from the previous week. The market reopens on Tuesday after the Labour Day holiday on Monday.
